newsitem.title: USA: Rebels surrender, others flee to end Texas siege.
newsitem.headline: Rebels surrender, others flee to end Texas siege.

text.p: A week-long standoff between police and renegade Texas separatists ended on Saturday when four of the once-defiant rebels surrendered and two others fled into the surrounding mountains, police said.
Texas Department of Public Safety spokesman Mike Cox told reporters that Republic of Texas leader Richard McLaren was among those who had given himself up without firing a shot.

Helicopters, bloodhounds and troopers on horses were combing the area in search of the two fugitives, whom Cox said were armed and wearing military-style camouflage outfits. He predicted they would be captured shortly.

The end to the tense siege came a few hours after McLaren's wife, Evelyn, left the rebels' tin-walled compound in the Davis Mountains in west Texas and surrendered. She told police the remaining Republic members, who say Texas is an independent nation, were ready to turn themselves in.

Cox said McLaren, who talked tough throughout the ordeal and vowed to fight to the death, was convinced to give up by the dozens of heavily-armed police who on Friday night had moved within a quarter-mile of what he called "the embassy."
"He was very much aware we had a very strong presence around his area," Cox said.
Cox said McLaren signed a document outlining the terms of the surrender, but got no concessions from Texas Ranger negotiator Capt. Barry Caver.
"There is no agreement other than they agreed to come out peacefully and they agreed to cease fire," Cox said. "There were no promises on the part of the Department of Public Safety."

The siege began on Sunday when Republic members took two hostages in retaliation for the arrest of their security chief. The hostages were later released, but six of the rebels face state felony charges arising from the kidnapping. Evelyn McLaren has been indicted on separate federal charges including bank and mail fraud, Cox said.

Estimates of up to 200 police poured into the area to surround the separatists' compound, backed by armoured personnel carriers, military helicopters, battering rams and bomb disposal equipment which Cox said would be used to defuse explosives planted by the Republic.

Cox said McLaren and top aide Richard "White Eagle" Otto were the first to surrender, followed by Gregg and Karen Paulson. Karen Paulson, he said, was thought to be a German citizen. McLaren, a 43-year-old vintner from Missouri, emerged from the compound wearing a cowboy hat, boots, jeans and a sports jacket.

The Republic of Texas, which claims to have thousands of members and ties to anti-government militia groups, believes the United States' 1845 annexation of Texas was illegal. Texas was an independent nation for nine years after breaking away from Mexico in 1836 in a rebellion McLaren likened to his own.

Before surrendering, Cox said the group performed a military-style ceremony laying down their arms in a circle on the ground. They had 10 rifles, including a couple of semi-automatic weapons, and up to 700 rounds of ammunition.
Cox said the DPS had "shown the world" how to handle sieges with anti-government groups.
"(There were) absolutely no shots fired. This has come down exactly as we wanted it to -- a peaceful resolution," he said.

The two men who disappeared into the mountains were thought to be Richard Keyes and Mike Matson, Cox said. Keyes has been accused of leading the Sunday kidnapping of two neighbours, but there are no charges against Matson, he said.
He said the Republic members would be questioned at the police command centre and later taken to jail in nearby Marfa, Texas.
